The integration of Ultra-High-Strength Engineered Cementitious Composites (UHS-ECC) with Fiber-Reinforced Polymer (FRP) bar/grid reinforcement can significantly enhance the flexural performance of marine infrastructure panels, leading to improved durability, reduced residual deflection, and stable hysteretic behavior under cyclic loading conditions. This enhancement will be achieved through a multi-faceted approach that includes:

1. Optimizing Matrix-Reinforcement Interaction:
   - Specific fiber orientations (0°, 45°, 90°) and volume fractions of FRP reinforcement (2%, 5%, 8%) will be evaluated to determine their impact on flexural performance.
   - Surface treatments such as etching with hydrofluoric acid or coating with silane will be applied to FRP bars/grids to increase bond strength by up to 30%.
   - Geometric configurations, including grid spacings of 50 mm and 100 mm and bar diameters of 6 mm and 10 mm, will be tested based on preliminary studies showing these configurations offer optimal mechanical properties.

2. Advanced Mix Design:
   - UHS-ECC mix design will incorporate specific binder types (e.g., high-performance cement with silica fume) and admixtures (e.g., superplasticizers at 0.5% dosage) to achieve enhanced tensile strength and ductility.
   - Microstructural compatibility between FRP and UHS-ECC will be optimized using advanced characterization techniques like Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) at 1 nm resolution and X-ray diffraction.

3. Multi-Scale Modeling and Simulation:
   - A nonlinear moment-curvature relationship model will be developed using finite element analysis (FEA) software like ABAQUS, incorporating machine learning algorithms to predict crack propagation patterns accurately.
   - Digital Image Correlation (DIC) will be employed alongside SEM and X-ray diffraction for comprehensive microstructural analysis, ensuring precise prediction and control of flexural performance.

4. Comprehensive Testing Protocols:
   - Cyclic loading tests will be conducted at frequencies of 0.5 Hz and 1 Hz, with 50 cycles per test, simulating wave-induced loading conditions.
   - Panels will undergo saltwater immersion for 30 days to replicate marine environments, followed by detailed assessments of flexural performance, durability, crack resistance measured by deflection at first cracking, energy dissipation, and post-loading deformation.

This can be achieved by optimizing key parameters of the matrix-reinforcement interaction, including fiber orientation and volume fraction of FRP reinforcement, mix design of UHS-ECC with specific binder types and admixtures, surface treatments for FRP bars/grids to enhance bond strength, and geometric configurations such as grid spacing and bar diameter. Comprehensive testing protocols will involve specific loading rates and frequencies for cyclic loading tests, environmental conditions simulating marine environments, and criteria for defining significant enhancements in flexural performance, durability, and other relevant metrics.

A functionally graded Fiber Reinforced Polymer (FRP) reinforcement system within Ultra-High-Strength Engineered Cementitious Composite (UHS-ECC) panels, featuring a gradient of stiffness and tensile capacity from the tensile face to the neutral axis, will be achieved by varying the type of FRP reinforcement. Specifically, the design will incorporate three layers of 10mm diameter Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) bars with a 2% reinforcement ratio closest to the tensile face, followed by two layers of 10mm diameter Basalt Fiber Reinforced Polymer (BFRP) bars with a 1.5% reinforcement ratio, and one layer of 10mm diameter Glass Fiber Reinforced Polymer (GFRP) bars with a 1% reinforcement ratio closest to the neutral axis. The CFRP bars will possess a tensile strength of 3500 MPa, an elastic modulus of 230 GPa, and an elongation at break of 1.5%; the BFRP bars will have a tensile strength of 1800 MPa, an elastic modulus of 80 GPa, and an elongation at break of 2.5%; and the GFRP bars will have a tensile strength of 1000 MPa, an elastic modulus of 50 GPa, and an elongation at break of 3%. This specific gradient is chosen to leverage the high strength and stiffness of CFRP at the tensile face to resist initial cracking, the moderate strength and modulus of BFRP to provide intermediate ductility, and the lower strength and modulus of GFRP near the neutral axis for strain compatibility. This arrangement will result in a 15% increase in energy absorption and a 20% reduction in crack width at peak load, calculated as the average value across multiple tested samples, compared to a UHS-ECC panel reinforced with the same total volume of conventional uniformly distributed FRP reinforcement (i.e., six layers of 10mm diameter CFRP bars with a total reinforcement ratio of 4.5% evenly distributed, also with the same properties of CFRP described previously). This enhancement will be evaluated after a 180-day accelerated aging process, where, after 28 days of curing under 20 degree temperature and 95% humidity, the panels will be subjected to 180 cycles of wetting (submerged in a 3.5% NaCl solution for 12 hours) and drying (at 40°C for 12 hours). The flexural performance will be assessed using a three-point bending test at a loading rate of 1 mm/min with a 700 mm support span. Crack widths will be measured at the center of the tensile surface of the beam using a high-resolution digital microscope, at a location aligned with the midpoint of the support span.

The underlying mechanism is that this functionally graded reinforcement will induce a gradual variation in material stiffness and ductility and enhance the progressive cracking behavior in ECC under flexural loading. Specifically, the flexural stiffness of the FRP reinforcement will gradually decrease from 230 GPa (CFRP) to 80 GPa (BFRP) to 50 GPa (GFRP) from the tensile face towards the neutral axis. This will lead to improved energy absorption and overall ductility of the UHS-ECC panel by effectively suppressing and distributing the cracks in the UHS-ECC matrix and preventing premature failure of the FRP and matrix. The gradually varied reinforcement design allows the composite to exhibit a more gradual transition from linear to nonlinear behavior, thus improving energy absorption capacity without compromising flexural strength. A numerical model based on cohesive zone modeling using a bilinear traction-separation law within a finite element framework (Abaqus software will be employed) will be used to simulate the strain distribution and quantify the interface stress between UHS-ECC and the different FRP reinforcement types. The cohesive zone model parameters, including the interface stiffness, cohesive strength, and critical separation displacement, will be determined based on the experimental results of single fiber pull out test and will be calibrated to match the test results. The mesh will be refined around the FRP-ECC interface to accurately capture the stress concentration. The UHS-ECC matrix material properties in the simulation will be defined as: compressive strength (90 MPa), tensile strength (8 MPa), elastic modulus (35 GPa), and fracture energy (1500 N/m). Interface parameters for each FRP-ECC combination (e.g. interface stiffness, cohesive strength, and critical separation displacement) will be determined using a separate set of single fiber pull-out tests. The stiffness and crack width will be measured at different load levels and compared between the functionally graded reinforced panels and uniformly reinforced panels to confirm this proposed mechanism.

The UHS-ECC mix will be designed using a binder content of 750 kg/m³, a water-to-binder ratio of 0.28, fine aggregate with particle size less than 200 um, and 1.5% volume of PVA fibers with a length of 8mm. The dimensions of the panel will be 100mm in height, 200mm in width, and 800mm in length.

This approach is novel as it combines functionally graded FRP reinforcement with UHS-ECC, a material system that has been previously demonstrated to have great potential for sustainable and durable infrastructure, especially in harsh marine environments. The use of specific FRP types with a carefully engineered gradient is a departure from previous studies that primarily focus on uniform FRP reinforcement or functionally graded cementitious materials, highlighting a novel advancement in material combination and application. The engineered gradual change in stiffness and ductility is designed to optimize the balance of strength and energy absorption, not previously explored to this extent with UHS-ECC for such application. Furthermore, unlike some other researches, we are utilizing a mix of high-performance and more common materials (CFRP, BFRP, GFRP) to provide insights into a more economically feasible application, as BFRP and GFRP are generally more cost-effective than CFRP. This research aims to address the limitations of conventional concrete structures, particularly in harsh marine environments, by providing a more sustainable and durable alternative with higher flexural performance and extended service life. The outcomes of this research may potentially reduce the reliance on other materials and construction methods, addressing limitations of conventional materials in achieving structural robustness and durability, and paving the way for more resource-efficient infrastructure designs. This will have potentially far-reaching implications for the construction industry by reducing maintenance and replacement costs and contributing to a more sustainable built environment.
